content: CBX1, also known as Chromobox protein homolog 1, is a protein in humans encoded by the CBX1 gene. The CBX1 protein is specifically localized to regions of heterochromatin within the genome. At these sites, it plays a critical role in mediating gene silencing, thereby regulating gene expression. To study the function of CBX1, model organisms have been utilized. A conditional knockout mouse line, named Cbx1tm1a(EUCOMM)Wtsi, was developed as part of the International Knockout Mouse Consortium program. This program is a large-scale mutagenesis initiative aimed at creating and distributing animal models of human diseases to researchers worldwide. The mouse line was generated at the Wellcome Trust Sanger Institute. Both male and female mice from this line underwent a standardized phenotypic screening process to assess the effects of CBX1 gene deletion. A total of 22 tests were conducted, and two distinct phenotypes were identified. Notably, no homozygous mutant mice survived beyond two weeks of age. Consequently, the remaining tests were performed on heterozygous mutant mice. Male heterozygous mice exhibited increased oxygen consumption (VO2), an elevated rate of carbon dioxide elimination, and higher energy expenditure. These findings were determined using indirect calorimetry, a method for measuring metabolic activity. CBX1 has been demonstrated to interact with several other proteins, including C11orf30, CBX3, CBX5, and SUV39H1. These interactions suggest its involvement in complex molecular pathways related to chromatin structure and function.
